title: Heat stroke (WMS and ACSM)
subject: emergency
summary: Heat stroke is a rectal temperature above 40 degrees C with CNS dysfunction. Cool first, transport second: start cold or ice-water immersion (or the fastest method available) within minutes, stop at about 38.3 to 38.8 degrees C, then manage organ injury. Antipyretics and dantrolene have no role.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Heat stroke: core (rectal) temperature above 40 degrees C with CNS dysfunction (confusion, irritability, ataxia, collapse, seizures, coma), during or after exertion (exertional) or passive heat exposure (classic, non-exertional).
Measure rectal temperature; oral, tympanic, temporal and axillary readings are inaccurate. If a rectal reading is not immediately possible, start cooling anyway.
Temperature may be below 40 degrees C on arrival after cooling in transit; CNS dysfunction after heat stress still means heat stroke until proven otherwise.
Heat exhaustion: weakness, fatigue, thirst, headache, nausea, dizziness and cramps without significant CNS dysfunction, usually with a temperature below 40 degrees C.

Differentials: sudden cardiac arrest, exercise-associated hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, head injury and postural collapse after exercise; with fever and coma also sepsis, meningitis, malaria, drug toxicity (sympathomimetic, anticholinergic, serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome) and thyroid storm.

sections.title: Cool first, transport second
items: Start whole-body cooling within minutes of collapse, on site or on arrival. Cooling rates above 0.15 degrees C per minute are desirable (above 0.08 acceptable); aim to reach a safe temperature within about 30 minutes.

Cold or ice-water immersion is the preferred method (WMS 2024, ACSM 2023): immerse the body to the neck, stir the water, add ice, and keep the head and airway supported above water. If ice water is not possible, use the coldest water available.

If immersion is impossible: tarp-assisted ice-water immersion, cold-water dousing, or rapidly rotated ice-water-soaked towels over the whole body. Evaporative cooling (spray and fan) is about half as fast and poor in humid heat. Ice packs to neck, axillae and groin alone are inadequate.

Stop active cooling at a rectal temperature of about 38.3 to 38.8 degrees C (WMS). Without continuous rectal monitoring, continue until mental status and vital signs normalise; if there is no improvement after 30 to 40 minutes, reassess the diagnosis.
Protect the airway (recovery position or intubation), give oxygen, and check glucose and sodium early. IV access and fluids must not delay or interrupt cooling.
If transfer is unavoidable before cooling is complete, keep cooling en route (ice-water towels, ice packs, chilled IV fluids as an adjunct, air conditioning at maximum).

sections.title: Supportive and hospital care
items: No antipyretics (paracetamol, NSAIDs) and no dantrolene: WMS recommends against any drug for lowering temperature in heat stroke.

Fluids: IV isotonic fluid for heat stroke with hypovolaemia, in small boluses with reassessment; avoid overload, especially in older patients. Check sodium before large volumes in endurance athletes (hyponatraemia). Switch to oral fluids once able to swallow.
Seizures, agitation or shivering that hinder cooling: IV benzodiazepine; intubate and ventilate if needed.
Anticipate rhabdomyolysis, AKI, hyperkalaemia, acute liver injury, DIC and hypoglycaemia; give ICU care for multi-organ dysfunction, with renal replacement therapy and blood products as required.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Blood count and platelets, electrolytes, calcium, phosphate, glucose, urea and creatinine, uric acid, AST, ALT, LDH, bilirubin, CK, blood and urine myoglobin, PT, aPTT, fibrinogen and degradation products, lactate and blood gas (ACSM).
Repeat CK, creatinine, liver tests and coagulation at least daily for 72 hours: kidney markers usually peak on day 1, while muscle and liver markers peak within about 4 days.

ECG and troponin; CT head if CNS dysfunction persists after cooling or there are focal signs; lumbar puncture if meningitis is possible (after cooling and a clotting check); malaria test and blood cultures where relevant.

sections.title: Disposition and return to activity
items: Admit heat stroke that needed hospital cooling or has any organ dysfunction; ICU for persistent CNS dysfunction, shock, respiratory failure, AKI, liver injury or DIC.

WMS: a healthy person with exertional heat stroke who is adequately cooled in the field and returns to baseline mental status and mobility within 2 hours may be released to self-care; all others go to hospital.
Heat exhaustion: rest in a cool place, loosen or remove clothing, oral fluids with salt; discharge when symptoms resolve.
After exertional heat stroke (ACSM): no exercise for at least 7 days after release, review at about 1 week with organ function tests, and start activity only when tests are normal.

Then return gradually, starting in a cool environment and increasing duration, intensity and heat exposure over 2 to 4 weeks. If this fails within 4 to 6 weeks, refer for specialist evaluation, which may include heat tolerance testing.

sections.title: Children, older adults and pregnancy
items: Children and lean athletes cool faster; monitor temperature closely to avoid overcooling. Never leave children in parked vehicles.

Classic heat stroke in older adults: comorbidities and drugs (diuretics, anticholinergics, antipsychotics, beta blockers) impair heat loss. Use the fastest method that monitoring allows; give IV fluids cautiously because of pulmonary oedema risk.
Pregnancy: cool rapidly with left lateral tilt and involve obstetrics for fetal assessment.
India: NCDC (NPCCHH) guidance favours evaporative cooling for frail classic cases and adds heatwave surveillance and public advisories; the cooling priorities are otherwise the same.

sections.title: Prevention
items: Use wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) to judge environmental heat risk, with the heat index as a second-line measure (WMS); modify or cancel activity when the risk is high (ACSM).
Acclimatise over 10 to 14 days of progressive heat exposure; even 1 week reduces physiological strain.
Drink to thirst rather than to a schedule, to avoid exercise-associated hyponatraemia.

Screen for risk factors (high BMI, previous heat illness, recent illness, heat-sensitising drugs), and have on-site ice-water immersion and rectal thermometers at events and workplaces with heat risk.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Transporting before cooling, or relying on ice packs and fans alone.
Using oral, tympanic or forehead temperature and missing heat stroke, or stopping cooling too early.
Giving antipyretics or dantrolene, or aggressive IV fluids that cause hyponatraemia or pulmonary oedema.
Labelling fever with coma as heat stroke without excluding sepsis, meningitis, malaria or drug toxicity.

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.dose: Adults 4 mg IV (0.1 mg/kg, maximum 4 mg); children 0.1 mg/kg IV (maximum 4 mg); may repeat once after 5 to 10 minutes
drugs.notes: Seizures, agitation or shivering that impede cooling. Watch for respiratory depression.

drugs.name: Midazolam
drugs.dose: 10 mg IM (5 mg if 13 to 40 kg) when there is no IV access

drugs.name: Isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline or balanced solution)
drugs.dose: Adults 250 to 500 mL IV boluses; children 10 to 20 mL/kg IV boluses; reassess after each
drugs.notes: Only for hypovolaemia or hypotension; check sodium first in endurance athletes. Chilled fluid is an adjunct, not a substitute for immersion.

drugs.name: Dextrose
drugs.dose: Adults 25 g IV (for example 250 mL of 10%); children 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg IV
drugs.notes: For glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L); recheck after 15 minutes.
